358.hook: Jacob wrestles all night, won't let go without a blessing, and limps away renamed

358.howItsDone: The Catechism points to Jacob's night at the river as a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and a triumph of perseverance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Reuben: seven years like a few days, and the sister nobody chose. Your line was leah was seen. A new week, and a long night.

In a side chapel of the church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris, there's a huge painting by Eugène Delacroix. A tree twists up into the sky. In front of it, two figures are locked together: a man, muscles straining, pushing with everything he has, and one with wings, standing almost calmly, a hand on the man's thigh. Twenty years have passed since Jacob ran from home. He's rich now, with wives, children, flocks. Tomorrow he has to face the brother who once planned to kill him, coming with four hundred men. Tonight, alone by a river, someone grabs him in the dark.
screen: `A PAINTING IN SAINT-SULPICE.` → `TWENTY YEARS, AND ESAU IS COMING.` → `ALONE BY A RIVER, IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the fight. Jacob sends his family across the river Jaboc and stays behind alone, and a man wrestles with him until the breaking of the day. Who is he? Genesis just says a man. The prophet Hosea later calls him an angel. Jacob, by morning, says he has seen God face to face. The text leaves it open, and so does Delacroix. Second, the hold. The stranger can't overcome him, so he touches the hollow of Jacob's thigh, and it's put out of joint. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let me go, for it is break of day. He answered: I will not let thee go except thou bless me." Injured, exhausted, and still holding on. Third, the name. The stranger asks, what is thy name? For the man who once said I am Esau to his father, the answer is a confession: Jacob. Heel-grabber. And the stranger says: "Thy name shall not be called Jacob, but Israel: for if thou hast been strong against God, how much more shalt thou prevail against men?" Israel, in Hebrew, sounds like one who strives with God, or God strives. A whole people will carry the name of a man who wrestled with God and wouldn't let go. Fourth, how the Church reads it. The Catechism calls this scene a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and a triumph of perseverance. Jacob doesn't win by pinning anyone. He wins by holding on, and asking. And he walks away at sunrise blessed, renamed, and limping.

359.title: Meeting Esau (Genesis 33)
359.hook: the brother he cheated runs and embraces him
359.howItsDone: Catholics pray "forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us" in every Our Father, and the Church teaches that being reconciled with others is bound up with being reconciled with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Israel: a night of wrestling, a new name, and a limp. Your line was I will not let thee go. This morning, Jacob limps toward his brother.

A name lights up on a phone: someone wronged years ago. A stomach can drop before a single word is read. Jacob has carried that dread for twenty years. When he fled, his brother was planning to kill him. Now there's Esau on the horizon, with four hundred men. Jacob has already sent wave after wave of gifts ahead, goats, sheep, camels, cattle, donkeys, hoping to soften him. He splits his family into groups. Then he limps out in front of all of them.

segments.voice: First, the bowing. Jacob bows to the ground seven times as he nears his brother. The one who stole a blessing that said nations would bow to him now bows, again and again, to the brother he cheated. Then the run. In the Douay-Rheims: "Then Esau ran to meet his brother, and embraced him: and clasping him fast about the neck, and kissing him, wept." The wronged one moves first. No speech, no list of grievances, no condition. Then the gifts. Jacob insists Esau keep the animals. Esau says, I have plenty, my brother; keep what is yours. And Jacob says something startling: seeing your face is like seeing the face of God. The night before, he wrestled God and called the place Phanuel, the face of God. Now he sees that face again, in the brother he feared. Last, the honesty. Genesis doesn't make it a fairy tale. Esau invites Jacob to travel with him; Jacob politely finds reasons to go his own way. The trust is new and fragile. But the brothers are at peace, and years later they stand together to bury their father. Some readers hear an echo in Luke's parable of the prodigal son: the father sees his son a long way off, runs, falls on his neck and kisses him. In both stories, the one with every right to stay away is the one who runs.

360.title: The coat and the dreams (Genesis 37:1–11)
360.hook: a favorite son, a colored coat, and brothers who can't speak peaceably
360.howItsDone: The Church reads the Joseph story in the weekday Mass during Lent, setting the brothers' envy beside the plot against Jesus in the Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting Esau: the wronged brother ran first. Your line was he ran to meet him. Today, the next generation, and the trouble starts again.

Some family albums have one: the kid in the middle of every picture. The one whose drawings went on the fridge, whose birthday got the bigger cake, who got away with things. A sibling can still name that kid, years later. Genesis has watched this pattern before. Isaac loved Esau more. Rebecca loved Jacob more. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. Now Jacob, old, called Israel, has twelve sons, and he doesn't even try to hide his favorite.
screen: `THE KID IN EVERY PICTURE.` → `A FAMILY OF FAVORITES.` → `TWELVE SONS, ONE FAVORITE.`

segments.voice: First, the favorite. Joseph is seventeen, the son of Rachel, the wife Jacob loved, born in Jacob's old age. He tends the flocks with his older half-brothers and brings his father a bad report about them. Then the coat. In the Douay-Rheims: "Now Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had him in his old age: and he made him a coat of divers colours. And his brethren seeing that he was loved by his father, more than all his sons, hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him." Could not speak peaceably. Not even hello. Honestly, nobody is sure what that coat looked like. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, gives it many colors. Some readers take the Hebrew, ketonet passim, as a long robe, the kind the second book of Samuel says a king's daughters wore. Either way, it wasn't work clothes. It said: this one doesn't do what you do. Then the dreams. Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves of grain bow down to his sheaf. Then that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. And he tells them, both times. The brothers hate him more. Even his father rebukes him: are your mother and I and your brothers to bow down to you? Last, the quiet line. The brothers envied him, Genesis says, but his father kept the matter in mind. Catholics may hear an echo in Luke, where Mary keeps things and ponders them in her heart. The father who caused the trouble also senses something in it he can't yet see.

361.title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
361.hook: the brothers sell Joseph for twenty pieces of silver
361.howItsDone: The Church keeps February 8, the feast of Saint Josephine Bakhita, a Sudanese woman sold into slavery as a child who became a Canossian sister, as a world day of prayer against human trafficking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ketonet passim: a favorite son, a coat, and brothers who couldn't say hello. Your line was the coat caused trouble. Today, the trouble comes due.

Jacob sends Joseph on an errand: go and see if your brothers are well, out with the flocks, and bring me word. It's a long walk from home. Joseph gets lost in the fields, and a stranger has to point him the right way. Then there he is on the last ridge, the boy in the coat, visible from far off. His brothers see him before he can see their faces. And one of them says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the dreamer cometh." By the time he reaches them, they've already decided.
screen: `GO AND SEE IF YOUR BROTHERS ARE WELL.` → `THE COAT, SEEN FROM FAR OFF.` → `BEHOLD THE DREAMER COMETH.`

segments.voice: First, the plot. Come, the brothers say, let's kill him, throw him into a pit, say a wild beast ate him, and see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the eldest, pushes back: don't kill him, just throw him in the pit. He planned, Genesis says, to come back later and rescue him. Then the pit. They strip off the coat, that coat, and throw him into an old cistern. It's empty, the text says. No water in it. And then, without a word of comment from Genesis, they sit down to eat bread. Then the sale. A caravan comes by, carrying spices down to Egypt. Judah speaks up: what profit is there in killing our brother? Let's sell him; he's our own flesh. They pull him out of the pit and, in the Douay-Rheims, "sold him to the Ismaelites, for twenty pieces of silver." Reuben comes back, finds the pit empty, and tears his clothes. Last, the lie. The brothers kill a young goat, dip the coat in its blood, and send it to their father: do you know this coat? Jacob, who once wore goatskins to deceive his own blind father, is now deceived by goat's blood on his son's coat. He tears his garments and refuses to be comforted. I will go down to my son mourning, he says. Church Fathers such as Ambrose read Joseph as a figure of Christ: the beloved son, sent by his father to his brothers, rejected by his own, sold for silver, and carried down into Egypt.

362.title: Prison (Genesis 39–40)
362.hook: a false accusation, prison, and a forgotten favor
362.howItsDone: The Joseph story is read at Mass on a weekday in Lent, and Psalm 105 (104 in the Douay numbering), which remembers Joseph in fetters, is among the psalms of the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bor: a dry cistern, a coat dipped in goat's blood, and a brother sold to traders bound for Egypt. Your line was sold by his own.

Egypt. Joseph is a slave now, still a young man, bought by an officer of Pharaoh named Potiphar. And something odd happens: everything he touches goes well. Soon he's running the whole house. Then his master's wife starts noticing him, day after day, and one day, when no one else is inside, she grabs him by his cloak. He runs, and leaves the cloak in her hand. She holds up the cloak and says he attacked her: the second time Joseph's clothes have been turned into a lie, after the coat in goat's blood. Potiphar believes her. Joseph goes to prison.

segments.voice: Read chapter thirty-nine slowly and one phrase keeps coming back: the Lord was with Joseph. It's there when he's a slave in Potiphar's house, when his master sees everything prospering in his hands, and twice in the prison. "But the Lord was with Joseph," the Douay-Rheims reads, and soon the keeper of the prison puts him in charge of the other prisoners. Not on the day he's made governor: in the slave quarters and the cell. The text never says God got him out. It says God was with him in it. Second, what Joseph does when no one is looking. He refused his master's wife with two reasons: it would betray the man who trusted him with everything, and it would be a sin against God. Nobody was watching. That was the whole test. Third, the forgotten favor. Two of Pharaoh's officials land in the same prison: the chief butler, who poured Pharaoh's wine, and the chief baker. Each has a dream. One morning Joseph sees their sad faces and asks why. Interpretations belong to God, he says, then tells them: in three days the butler goes back to his post, and the baker dies. Both come true. Joseph asks the butler one thing: remember me to Pharaoh. And the chapter ends flatly. The butler forgot him. Two full years go by. Centuries later, a psalm remembers this stretch: his feet humbled in fetters, iron around him, until God's word came. The chapter doesn't hurry past the waiting, and it never calls it wasted.

363.title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41)
363.hook: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner becomes governor
363.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Joseph as patron of the universal Church, of workers and of families, and the old phrase Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to him, especially in March, the month traditionally given to Saint Joseph.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prison: a false charge, a cell, and a butler who forgot. Your line was the lord was with joseph.

Two years later, Pharaoh has a nightmare. By the Nile, seven sleek, fat cows come up out of the river. Then seven thin ones, all bone, eat the fat ones and look no better afterward. He wakes, sleeps, and dreams again: seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. Every wise man in Egypt is summoned. Nobody can explain it. Then the butler, the one who forgot, suddenly remembers a young Hebrew in prison who read dreams. Joseph is pulled out of the dungeon, shaved, given clean clothes, and stood before the king.
screen: `SEVEN FAT COWS, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Pharaoh says he hears Joseph can read dreams. Joseph's first words turn that around: it isn't in him; God will give Pharaoh his answer. Then the meaning. Seven years of plenty are coming to Egypt, and after them seven years of famine so heavy the good years will be forgotten. The dream came twice, Joseph says, because the thing is settled. Then, unasked, he doesn't stop at the warning; he gives a plan. Find a wise man. Set overseers over the land. Store a fifth of the harvest in the cities in each good year, so that when the lean years come, the country doesn't die. Pharaoh asks his court, in effect, where would we find another man with the spirit of God in him? He puts his ring on Joseph's hand, dresses him in fine linen, hangs a gold chain around his neck, and makes him governor of all Egypt. Joseph is thirty. He was seventeen when his brothers sold him. Then it plays out exactly: seven fat years, grain piled up like the sand of the sea, then famine in every land. The people cry to Pharaoh for bread, and he answers in three words: "Go to Joseph." Catholics have borrowed that line for a different Joseph. Saint Joseph, the husband of Mary, also listened to dreams and also took his family down to Egypt, and in 1870 Pope Pius the Ninth named him patron of the whole Church. In Latin, Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to him.

If it's already lean, notice what a full one left you. If you pray, offer the full years and the lean ones to God; if you don't, just sit with the thought of both.

364.title: The brothers come for grain (Genesis 42–44)
364.hook: Joseph tests them, and Judah offers himself for Benjamin
364.howItsDone: Some Catholic preaching sees in Judah's offer to take Benjamin's place a picture of Christ, whom the Book of the Apocalypse calls the lion of the tribe of Juda.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner made governor. Your line was plan for the lean years.

The famine reaches Canaan. Old Jacob hears there's grain in Egypt and sends ten of his sons to buy some. Not the youngest, Benjamin, Rachel's last son; Jacob won't risk him. The ten bow, faces to the ground, before the governor of Egypt, with no idea who he is: an Egyptian name, Egyptian clothes, an interpreter between them. He knows them at once, and remembers the dreams: sheaves bowing down to his. What would you do with your brothers in that room?
screen: `TEN BROTHERS GO DOWN TO EGYPT.` → `THEY BOW, AND DON'T KNOW HIM.` → `HE KNOWS THEM AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Joseph doesn't reveal himself. He tests them. First, he calls them spies and holds them three days. Then he keeps one brother, Simeon, and sends the rest home: bring your youngest back, and I'll believe you. In front of him, thinking he can't understand, they talk in their own language: we are guilty about our brother; we saw his distress when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. Joseph turns aside and weeps. Second, the hard road home. Jacob refuses to send Benjamin. Only when the grain runs out does Judah speak up: put the boy in my hands, and if I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever. Third, the trap. In Egypt, a feast, then a silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. The steward finds it, and the governor's verdict is simple: the one with the cup becomes my slave; the rest of you can go home. They've stood at this door before: years ago they let Rachel's son be carried off to Egypt and went home without him. They could do it again, and legally. Fourth, Judah steps forward. He tells the whole story, the old father, the lost son, how the father's life is bound up in the boy's, and then he asks: let me stay as your slave instead; let the boy go home. This is the same Judah who once said sell him for silver. Matthew's Gospel traces Jesus's family through him. Look back over the week: a wrestler renamed Israel, Esau running, the coat, the pit, the prison, the dreams. A family that kept breaking, and now someone stands in the gap.
screen: `SPIES! THEY CONFESS THEIR OLD GUILT.` · `JUDAH PLEDGES HIMSELF FOR THE BOY.` · `A SILVER CUP IN BENJAMIN'S SACK.` · `TAKE ME INSTEAD OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Think of someone carrying something heavy right now: a coworker buried in a deadline, a parent with a sick kid, a friend facing a hard phone call. Picture taking their place for an hour, a covered shift, a seat in the waiting room. If you pray, hold that person before God, the way Judah held his brother before the governor; if you don't, keep them in mind for a minute.
